Lorsque Nina Gonzalez* s'adresse au publ: When Nina Gonzalez* speaks to the public or the media on behalf of the Women’s Committee of the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC), she always wears a mask and glasses.
L'idée est que personne ne voie son visa: The idea is that no one sees her face, but that her voice can be heard. Like tens of thousands of people in Canada, some 500,000 according to federal government statistics, Nina lives in the shadows because she has no papers.
Cette militante des droits des femmes es: This women’s rights activist arrived in Montréal in 2008 with her daughter, who was 14 at the time. Sixteen years later, at 50, Nina looks like a young girl, which matches her style of dress. Her eyes are big, and so is her smile, features that people generally can’t see.
Au Canada, elle pensait avoir gagné à la: In Canada, she thought she had won the lottery, discovering a peace she had never known. She had suffered physical and psychological violence, abandonment and constant precarity in Bogotá, and leaving Colombia gave her a new lease on life.
Mais savourer cette paix a été de courte: But enjoying that peace was short-lived for this single mother, who moves her hands eloquently as she speaks. Badly advised by an immigration consultant of Latin American origin, she submitted a refugee claim that was not real. Her application and her daughter’s were rejected.
Le jour de notre rencontre, Nina a oubli: The day we meet, Nina has forgotten her mask at home. Confident, she decides to go ahead with the interview. It is the first time we see her face, framed by her curly hair.
Elle est joviale, en dépit du fait que s: She is cheerful, even though her eyes show fatigue. You can tell she wants to tell us her story. The more she talks, the more at ease she seems. She smiles almost throughout the entire interview.
Son temps avec nous est compté car elle: Her time with us is limited, because in less than an hour she has to get to a house in Outremont where she is cleaning that day.
C’est l'un des emplois <em>cash </em>que: It is one of the cash jobs the activist does regularly. Yet while waiting for an answer on her asylum claim, she managed to earn a care attendant diploma, which gave her experience in caring for seniors.
Malgré le temps contraint de notre renco: Despite the limited time we have, Nina speaks slowly and frankly. Her emotions are front and centre. She smiles when she talks about her activism on behalf of women and undocumented people, a commitment that makes her feel fulfilled. Her eyes reveal the pain she carries inside.
« Je suis arrivée à Montréal en plein ét: “I arrived in Montréal in the middle of summer. It was fantastic,” she says, looking out the café window at the 9 a.m. sun on a spring day that feels more like summer.
« Je viens d'un milieu où il y a eu beau: “I come from an environment where there was a lot of violence. Economic, physical and family violence. Coming to Montréal was an opportunity, a chance to try my luck. I had never been on a plane in my life. When the opportunity came up, because an acquaintance lent me money, I didn’t think twice. The situation I was living in in Colombia with my daughter was very difficult.”
Pour venir à Montréal, Nina a reçu envir: To come to Montréal, Nina received about $2,000 from this acquaintance, whose identity she prefers not to reveal. “It was money I had never seen, a fortune,” she adds.
Son voyage n'a pas été direct. Elle a d': Her journey was not direct. She first had to stop over in Mexico, where she obtained fake Mexican documents so she could travel to Montréal without a visa. Colombians are in fact required to present that golden ticket to enter the country. Once she arrived at Montréal’s Trudeau airport, she declared that she was Colombian and that she was in Canada to claim asylum.
Rappelons que le gouvernement de Stephen: It should be noted that Stephen Harper’s government imposed a visa requirement on Mexicans in 2009, a measure that was lifted by the Trudeau government in 2016 and reimposed in 2024 by Trudeau himself.
« La vérité, c'est que je n'étais pas co: “The truth is, I wasn’t aware of what I was doing. I was 34 and my daughter was 14. I was desperate because I wanted to get out of the violence I was living in,” she says.
À son arrivée à Saint-Léonard, Nina est: When she arrived in Saint-Léonard, Nina was happy. “When I saw the city, the social environment, the dynamic of Montréal, I was glad. But I also started running into difficulties. The first was the scam by the person who advised me on my file. A Colombian who spoke Spanish, which is what I needed because I hadn’t learned French yet,” says the activist, who now gives press conferences in the language of Dany Laferrière.
« C'est ce qui arrive à de nombreux immi: “It’s what happens to a lot of immigrants,” she adds. “When you come here, you meet many lawyers and immigration consultants, in quotation marks, but they’re people who just want to take your money. They have no ethics, no human values, they only damage a person’s life, and that’s what happened to me,” she laments. Her eyes well up; she tries to hide it by continuing the conversation.
Le consultant en immigration lui a suggé: The immigration consultant suggested she file a false refugee claim (a story that wasn’t real), explaining that she would have a good chance of having it accepted.
« Je sais que je suis également coupable: “I know I’m also guilty, because I accepted his suggestion and, in doing so, I made a very big mistake. My credibility is seriously damaged in the eyes of the immigration authorities,” she says with regret.
Elle réfléchit à haute voix : « On vient: She reflects out loud: “We come from countries and from a context of precarity. Many absences. I grew up with my grandmother and she instilled a lot of values in me, but what happens is that when you meet these people who say they want to help you, they exploit precarity, ignorance and desperation and just take your money.” One day, she even paid $100 to have an immigration document read to her in French.
Nina a versé à ce premier conseiller env: Nina paid this first adviser about $3,000. “I dare say that in the end, these people are a kind of mafia, because they ruin your life.”
Comme c'est souvent le cas dans la vie d: As is often the case in the lives of asylum seekers, waiting for an answer from Immigration is part of daily life. But Nina didn’t give up. With no experience in the field, she completed a certificate as a patient care attendant and worked in care homes for seniors. Her daughter went to school and had become part of her community.
« En 2011, j'ai eu mon audience et je do: “In 2011, I had my hearing, and I have to say that as an asylum seeker, you’re treated like a criminal. I don’t know a single person who came to claim asylum who told me they were treated well.”
Après l'audience, sa demande d'asile a é: After the hearing, her asylum claim was rejected. Advised by a new immigration lawyer, Nina appealed the decision to the Federal Court, and the answer was again a rejection.
Elle a ensuite soumis un dossier à l’exa: She then submitted a file for a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA), which allows people who are to be removed from Canada to request protection from the host country. It involves describing the risks they would face if deported. People whose PRRA application is approved can stay in the country.
Pour cette procédure, Nina s'est appuyée: For this procedure, Nina relied on a recommendation from another Latin American person. This acquaintance told her he had contacts within the immigration department.
« J’en reviens à la même chose et c'est: “I come back to the same thing, and this is advice for the people who will read your article: you think things here are like in your country, in your society. That there’s no need to wait in line, and so on... I arrived with those beliefs. And that’s how I fell into the same trap. I believed this person who told me he would help me get my residency and who ended up stealing $13,000 from me.”
C'était une période très difficile, avou: It was a very difficult time, Nina admits. “And I’m not talking about the money, because at this stage of life, you know it comes and goes. It’s the emotional harm that dragged my daughter and me to the bottom,” she says, wiping away her tears.
Fin 2014, alors que toutes les démarches: In late 2014, when every possible avenue for staying in Canada had been refused, except for a humanitarian residency application that Nina González had not yet submitted, mother and daughter received a summons from Immigration Canada.
« Ils ont eu la cruauté de fixer la date: “They were cruel enough to set my deportation date on the same day as my birthday, that is, in January. I told them at work what was happening, because I still had implied status. My supervisor, a nurse at the retirement home, got angry and cried with me. I was surprised by that love. She asked me how she could help me, but I didn’t really know how.”
Nina ignorait qu'elle était éligible à d: Nina didn’t know she was eligible to become a foreign worker, because the company she worked for could have submitted an application. “It’s a solid group present all over Montréal, but unfortunately I didn’t know I had that possibility, and that’s how I disappeared.”
C'est ainsi qu'a commencé une autre étap: That is how another chapter began for Nina and her daughter in Canada: life in the shadows.
« Ma fille n'a même pas pu terminer le s: “My daughter couldn’t even finish high school, and all of that weighed on me. She worked, like me. She looked after babies. She worked very hard. At one point, she thought the best thing for her was to go back to Colombia, but the night before the deportation date, we were at home, trying to watch a movie to calm ourselves. The truth is, we couldn’t separate, because we’ve always been together. ‘Whatever happens, Mom, we’re staying together,’ she told me that night,” she recalls, her voice trembling.
La clandestinité et l'isolement ont entr: Living in hiding and isolation led to a deterioration of Nina González’s mental health; she suffered from severe depression.
« C'est très dur. C'est la vie d'un être: “It’s very hard. It’s a human being’s life. We’re talking about years. Not one, not two, not three, but 10, 15, 20 years that many undocumented immigrants spend in Canada. Personally, I have no roots in Colombia, I miss nothing there, because I’ve never belonged anywhere. There’s no family circle, only violence and abuse.”

En 2018, Nina González est entrée en con: In 2018, Nina González got in touch with the Women’s Committee of the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC) through a friend. Like many of the women she talks with today in her role as community companion, earning trust was an arduous task.
« Lorsque je suis arrivée au comité, j'a: “When I got to the committee, I started to see how the work operated and I realized I could make my voice heard. The committee allowed me to express my pain. I felt recognized,” she says in a relieved tone.
Victime de harcèlement sexuel par un hom: A victim of sexual harassment by a man at one of the jobs she held in Montréal, Nina was able to confide in a group of women. Her voice became part of a set of testimonies presented by the Women’s Committee of the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC) to the Ministry of Labour and the Commission des normes, de l’équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST), as part of a brief so that women without status can file complaints with the relevant authorities.
« Cet aspect a également été très trauma: “That was also very traumatic for me. And I put up with it for a long time because I had no choice. But one day, I couldn’t take it anymore because the man became very aggressive. It reminded me of what I had lived through in Colombia. In the middle of winter, without really knowing what had happened, I left my job without a coat, nothing, just my work apron.”
Au sein du comité des femmes, Nina appre: Within the women’s committee, Nina learns that there are different levels of harassment and that victims can be young or older women.
« Nous avons entendu parler de cas de La: “We heard about cases of Latinas, African women, women from diverse backgrounds, women in their sixties, who were victims of abuse. Often, we’re not aware of what’s happening to us. Hearing those stories hurt me deeply, and I still can’t find the words when it’s my turn to say that I, too, was a victim.”
Retrouver la confiance a également fait: Regaining confidence was also part of Nina’s learning curve as an activist.
« Ce n'est pas facile, car j'ai toujours: “It’s not easy, because I’m always afraid. But I was surprised to see that I had abilities. It’s thanks to the committee’s community coordinator, Viviana, that I discovered it. I built bonds of trust and I feel happy. I feel fulfilled, I no longer feel so alone,” she says gladly, a smile in her eyes.
« Aujourd'hui, je peux parler pour ceux: “Today, I can speak for those who have no voice, for women like me, like my daughter, who are alone, isolated. I found a strength and a courage that isn’t even rage, because of physical violence, government violence, economic violence. It’s hard to be a woman. It hurts. I don’t show my face, I don’t give my name, but I give my voice and my strength.”
Nina regarde l'heure sur son cellulaire,: Nina checks the time on her cellphone; she will soon have to head to work. She complains of a pain in her shoulder.
« J'attends un rendez-vous depuis des mo: “I’ve been waiting months for an appointment at Médecins du Monde. I’ve been cleaning for 16 years and I’m already 50. It’s starting to weigh on me,” she confides.
La plainte concernant sa douleur ne dure: The complaint about her pain doesn’t last long. Nina immediately brings up the regularization program announced by the federal government in 2021, about which we still have no new details to date.
Le gouvernement a promis une annonce à c: The government promised an announcement on the subject by the end of spring. But the month of May is coming to an end and undocumented people don’t know how the measure will be applied, or whether it will be approved.
« Je ne pense pas que les gens comprenne: “I don’t think people understand that undocumented people don’t have a bank account, that they don’t have access to subsidized medical care, that they don’t have assistance plans, retirement plans. I used to ride a bike, but I don’t want to anymore, because two or three years ago, the police started handing out fines on bike paths and I’m at risk, even for things as basic as that,” Nina laments.
Malgré cela, elle vit sa vie du mieux qu: Despite this, she lives her life as best she can. “There are days when I’m low. There are moments at night when I can’t sleep. I’m integrated, I speak French. My daughter, who is 29, will get her permanent residency, because we separated our files and she applied on humanitarian grounds, which makes me happy.”
Nina continuera à être active dans sa lu: Nina will keep up her fight, and the fight of everyone without status. She doesn’t show her face, but she will keep making her voice heard.
